case_analysis.focal_point: Whether noncitizen asylum seekers and an assisting nonprofit may sue DHS in federal district court under the APA and Constitution to challenge alleged “turnbacks”/obstruction of access to the asylum process at or near the border, or whether immigration-channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions require dismissal because such claims must proceed (if at all) only through the INA’s limited review schemes.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the Immigration and Nationality Act’s jurisdiction-channeling/jurisdiction-stripping provisions (commonly including 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and related limits on review of removal-related decisions) and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 702, 704), with constitutional overlay (Suspension Clause/Due Process) implicated by the parties’ reliance on DHS v. Thuraissigiam; the dispute also implicates statutory asylum-access provisions (8 U.S.C. § 1158) insofar as respondents frame a right to apply for asylum and to be processed.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government (Secretary Noem/DHS) argues that respondents’ challenge is, in substance, an attack on the Executive’s border and removal screening operations that Congress has committed to the INA’s specialized review system, and that § 1252 (and related doctrines) bars district-court jurisdiction over systemic claims seeking to control how DHS processes or refuses to process would-be applicants at the border; petitioners invoke Supreme Court cases like DHS v. Thuraissigiam to emphasize Congress’s power to limit judicial review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens and to confine challenges to the narrow procedures Congress authorized, foreclosing broad APA/constitutional suits that would effectively expand review beyond what the INA permits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Al Otro Lado and the individual respondents contend the case is not a collateral attack on removal orders but a challenge to unlawful obstruction of access to the statutory asylum process (and related constitutional minima), including policies/practices that prevent people from presenting or pursuing asylum claims in the first place; they argue the INA’s channeling provisions should not be read to preclude district-court review of systemic, pre-removal barriers to applying for asylum (especially where no removal order or meaningful administrative record exists), that the APA supplies a cause of action to set aside agency action contrary to law, and that petitioners’ reliance on Thuraissigiam (a habeas challenge to expedited removal) is misplaced because it addressed post-screening review limits rather than an affirmative, front-end denial of access to the asylum process.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
Microsoft Corp. v. European Community, 136 S. Ct. 2090 (2016) (as quoted/used in the provided excerpt for distinguishing arguments)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s “no proceeding, no forum” argument is the most forceful, and I accept the premise for purposes of a narrow disposition: even if §§ 1252(a)(5) and (b)(9) do not practically channel these front-end turnback claims into a petition for review, that does not authorize a district court to issue the particular systemic relief sought here. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, the requested programmatic injunction would necessarily “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV inspection/expedited-removal mechanisms, bringing § 1252(f)(1) into play, and Aleman Gonzalez confirms Congress meant to bar lower-court systemwide injunctions of this kind. Justice Sotomayor’s accountability-vacuum concern cannot justify using constitutional avoidance to read around an express anti-injunction provision; Congress provided limited review routes (including § 1252(e)), and Thuraissigiam reinforces that courts may not expand review beyond what the INA permits simply to ensure an APA forum. On minimalist grounds, we should hold only that the district court lacked jurisdiction to grant this broad relief, leaving open whatever narrower, as-applied or expressly authorized challenges Congress preserved.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s “no proceeding, no forum” contention does not overcome the enacted text: § 1252(b)(9) reaches claims “arising from any action taken… to remove an alien,” and a suit seeking to compel DHS to accept and process would-be entrants into particular screening paths challenges actions integral to the statutory removal/inspection machinery in § 1225. Even if one doubts (b)(9) in some edge case, Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point about § 1252(f)(1) is independently dispositive for the programmatic injunctive relief sought here because it would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, which Aleman Gonzalez reinforces. Jennings’s warning against overreading (b)(9) does not license an APA end-run where Congress has specified narrow review routes (including § 1252(e)) and declared them exclusive; under Thuraissigiam, the absence of broader review for arriving, non-admitted aliens is not a defect courts may cure by expanding jurisdiction. I therefore see no basis, under an originalist and textualist approach, to invoke constitutional-avoidance to create a district-court forum Congress did not provide.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “no proceeding, no forum” argument is the most substantial, but it cannot overcome the separate and express bar in § 1252(f)(1): even if one doubts § 1252(b)(9) reaches every pre-proceeding claim, the programmatic relief respondents seek would necessarily “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV inspection/screening under § 1225, exactly as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize and as Aleman Gonzalez confirms. Justice Sotomayor’s accountability-vacuum concern does not authorize us to use constitutional avoidance to create APA jurisdiction where Congress instead provided narrow, specified review avenues in § 1252(e), including § 1252(e)(3) for certain systemic challenges, and otherwise curtailed district-court supervision. Jennings’ warning against letting (b)(9) swallow all immigration-adjacent claims has force, but this suit is not collateral; it is aimed at controlling the front-end pipeline, and under Reno v. AADC we should be wary of artful pleading to evade Congress’s channeling and anti-injunction scheme. Thuraissigiam does not decide this precise posture, but it reinforces that Congress may sharply confine review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens, undercutting the premise that we must strain § 1252 to guarantee a broad APA forum.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that § 1252(f)(1), especially after Aleman Gonzalez, is a serious constraint on district courts issuing sweeping, systemwide injunctions that effectively supervise Part IV border processing. But that remedy-limit does not answer Justice Kagan’s antecedent “no proceeding, no forum” problem: if the government’s alleged front-end obstruction prevents any removal proceeding or asylum application from ever coming into existence, reading § 1252(b)(9) and (g) to channel the claim would functionally eliminate review without a clear statement, in tension with Jennings’ warning against letting (b)(9) swallow everything. Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s reliance on Thuraissigiam is incomplete here because that case assumed the government had already initiated expedited removal and screening; it does not clearly authorize insulating an alleged refusal to accept or process asylum requests (an APA § 706(1) “unlawfully withheld” theory) from any forum. I can accept that the injunction must be narrowed to avoid “enjoin[ing] or restrain[ing] the operation” of Part IV, but I would not extend § 1252 to bar all district-court jurisdiction over threshold access-to-process claims where Congress mandated a procedure and provided no realistic alternative remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is remedial: a sweeping order that effectively rewrites or halts front-end inspection/screening could “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV and run headlong into § 1252(f)(1) as construed in Aleman Gonzalez, so I accept that broad programmatic injunctive relief is likely unavailable. But that does not answer the antecedent jurisdictional question: as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson emphasize, reading § 1252(a)(5) and (b)(9) to swallow an alleged threshold refusal to accept asylum applications risks creating a no-forum gap without a clear textual statement, especially where there is no proceeding, record, or order to channel into a petition for review. Thuraissigiam, invoked by Justices Thomas and Alito, confirms Congress can tightly limit review after expedited-removal screening has begun, but it does not squarely authorize insulating an alleged front-end obstruction of § 1158 from any judicial testing at all. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, I would preserve some district-court jurisdiction for narrowly tailored, non-systemic relief (or declaratory relief) while recognizing § 1252(f)(1) sharply limits what remedies a court may impose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “no proceeding, no forum” argument is the most serious, but on the text Congress wrote it does not defeat jurisdiction-stripping here: § 1252(b)(9) covers questions “arising from any action taken … to remove an alien,” which naturally includes front-end inspection and screening steps that determine whether removal processing begins and in what form. Even assuming some antecedent claims might sit at the periphery of (b)(9) under Jennings, Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that § 1252(f)(1) independently bars the programmatic injunction sought because it would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, as Aleman Gonzalez confirms, without making that prohibition turn on whether a removal order already exists. Justice Sotomayor’s accountability-vacuum concern cannot justify using constitutional avoidance to rewrite these express limits; Congress provided narrow, specified review paths in § 1252(e), and Thuraissigiam reinforces that courts may not expand review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens via the APA when Congress has tightly channeled it. I would therefore reverse on the limited ground that the district court lacked jurisdiction to issue the systemic injunctive relief requested, leaving open whatever individualized relief Congress expressly authorizes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s “no proceeding, no forum” concern is serious, but it cannot overcome the separate, express bar in § 1252(f)(1) on lower-court relief that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV; as the Chief Justice stresses, the practical effect of respondents’ requested systemic order is precisely to supervise and restructure that front-end machinery. Aleman Gonzalez confirms (f)(1) has real bite against programmatic injunctions, and constitutional-avoidance cannot be used to read around that clear anti-injunction command. Even if Jennings counsels against an overbroad use of § 1252(b)(9), that does not create affirmative district-court APA authority where (f)(1) independently forecloses the remedy sought, and Thuraissigiam supports Congress’s latitude to confine review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens without courts supplying an APA “backstop.” I remain open, as the Chief suggests, to a minimalist disposition focused on remedy/jurisdiction for systemic relief, without resolving every conceivable as-applied or statutorily authorized alternative path.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: if there is “no proceeding, no forum,” reading § 1252(b)(9) broadly could create an accountability gap. But the enacted text—claims “arising from any action taken … to remove an alien”—naturally reaches the front-end inspection/screening steps that implement Part IV’s removal machinery, and Congress’s decision to provide only narrow review in § 1252(e) is strong evidence it meant to foreclose broader APA district-court routes. Independently, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the systemic injunction sought would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, which § 1252(f)(1) expressly forbids and Aleman Gonzalez confirms cannot be evaded by recasting the challenge as “access” rather than “operation.” Jennings’s caution against (b)(9) swallowing everything does not fit a suit whose object is to supervise the functioning of the removal/inspection pipeline itself, and Thuraissigiam counsels against using avoidance to expand review beyond what the INA authorizes for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s § 1252(f)(1) point is the strongest obstacle, and I agree Aleman Gonzalez counsels against sweeping, programmatic injunctions that effectively re-engineer Part IV’s inspection/expedited-removal machinery. But I do not accept the premise—pressed by Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett under § 1252(b)(9)—that an alleged front-end refusal to allow access to the statutory asylum-application channel necessarily “arises from” action “to remove” when, on respondents’ theory, the government is preventing any proceeding, record, or order from coming into being; Jennings cautioned against letting (b)(9) swallow claims not meaningfully tethered to an actual removal process. Reading (f)(1) to bar any district-court jurisdiction over threshold “action unlawfully withheld” claims risks converting an anti-injunction provision into a de facto no-review rule without a clear statement, especially where § 1252(e)’s narrow review paths do not realistically reach these antecedent blockade allegations. On a pragmatic, process-fairness approach, I would preserve some judicial forum for these claims while recognizing that the remedy, if any, must be narrowly tailored to avoid enjoining the general “operation” of Part IV.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252 is written to channel and, in key respects, preclude district-court review of claims that in substance seek to supervise or restrain how DHS administers inspection, expedited removal, and related screening at the border, and respondents’ requested systemic relief would effectively “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV provisions such as § 1225, triggering § 1252(f)(1) and reinforcing Congress’s channeling design. Reno v. AADC instructs that § 1252’s limits are to be taken seriously as a jurisdictional scheme, not evaded by reframing removal-related challenges as broader constitutional or APA claims. Although respondents emphasize pre-removal “access to process,” the practical effect is to mandate changes to DHS’s border-processing operations that Congress has largely committed to the INA’s limited review mechanisms (including § 1252(e)’s narrow avenues), and Thuraissigiam confirms Congress’s authority to confine review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens. Given institutional and federalism concerns, the narrower, precedent-faithful course is dismissal for lack of district-court jurisdiction, leaving any review to the INA’s specified pathways (if available).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and, where specified, precludes judicial review outside its exclusive scheme: § 1252(a)(5) makes a petition for review the “sole and exclusive means” for review of removal orders, and § 1252(b)(9) broadly consolidates “all questions of law and fact” “arising from” actions taken to remove an alien. Respondents’ APA/constitutional challenge to alleged border “turnbacks” is, in substance, an effort to control DHS’s removal-screening and processing operations and therefore falls within Congress’s channeling choice rather than district-court APA review. In Jennings v. Rodriguez, this Court rejected attempts to evade § 1252(b)(9) through artful pleading, and DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms Congress may sharply limit review for arriving, non-admitted aliens without violating the Constitution. Because the APA cannot supply jurisdiction or a cause of action where Congress has expressly displaced review, the district court must dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s jurisdiction-channeling and jurisdiction-stripping scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 is written broadly to preclude district-court suits that, in substance, seek to supervise or restructure DHS’s border screening and admission/removal processes, and respondents’ requested relief would do exactly that. Where Congress has provided narrow, specific avenues for review—particularly for expedited removal and related screening determinations—it is not the role of courts to expand review via the APA (5 U.S.C. §§ 702, 704) or generalized constitutional claims, especially for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms Congress’s authority to confine judicial review for such individuals and cautions against using constitutional theories to obtain broader process than the INA permits. Permitting systemic “turnback” challenges in district court would undermine the practical operation of the statutory scheme and invite circumvention of the INA’s carefully limited review provisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252’s channeling provisions should not be read to foreclose all district-court review of front-end, systemic practices that prevent noncitizens from ever invoking the statutory right to apply for asylum under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1), particularly where there is no removal order and thus no meaningful path into the INA’s limited review schemes. Under the APA, an agency’s refusal to accept or process asylum requests can constitute unlawfully “withheld” action reviewable under 5 U.S.C. § 706(1), and the Constitution counsels against construing jurisdiction-stripping to leave vulnerable people without any forum to challenge arbitrary obstruction of access to the asylum process. DHS v. Thuraissigiam is not controlling because it addressed Congress’s limits on habeas review after expedited-removal screening, not claims that DHS is denying access to the screening and application process in the first place. Construing § 1252 (including § 1252(e)(3)) to require dismissal here would risk insulating unlawful turnback policies from any effective judicial check, contrary to basic principles of fairness and access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252’s channeling provisions—especially § 1252(a)(5) and § 1252(b)(9)—are textually tied to “judicial review of an order of removal” and to claims that “aris[e] from” removal proceedings, and a front-end “turnback” practice that prevents people from presenting themselves for the asylum process at all is not naturally read as review of, or arising from, a removal proceeding. Nor does § 1252(e) supply an alternative exclusive pathway for these claims: § 1252(e)(3) is aimed at challenges to the legality of the expedited-removal “system” in the District of Columbia on a tight timetable, and § 1252(e)(2) narrowly limits habeas review for persons already placed in expedited removal—leaving a serious workability and constitutional-avoidance problem if district courts cannot hear any claim where DHS allegedly blocks access before any record or proceeding exists. Thuraissigiam upheld Congress’s restriction of post-screening review for an arriving noncitizen already in expedited removal, but it did not decide that the INA forecloses all APA/constitutional suits challenging a policy that obstructs access to the statutory right to “apply for asylum” under § 1158 in the first instance. Reading § 1252 to bar these systemic, pre-processing obstruction claims would overextend the stripping language beyond its coherent subject (removal-order review) and would effectively immunize non-proceeding conduct from judicial review without a clear statement from Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s channeling provisions are written broadly, and § 1252(b)(9) in particular consolidates into the INA review scheme claims “arising from” the government’s removal process; a district-court APA suit seeking to control DHS’s front-end screening/inspection practices at the border is, in substance, an effort to reshape how removal and related screening decisions are conducted. Section 1252(g), as construed in Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, further strips jurisdiction over claims arising from decisions or actions to “commence proceedings” or “execute removal orders,” and respondents’ requested systemic relief would necessarily intrude on those prosecutorial and screening choices in a way Congress has channeled away from district courts. While Jennings v. Rodriguez cautions against reading § 1252(b)(9) to swallow all immigration-related claims, respondents here seek precisely the sort of programmatic, preemptive judicial supervision of removal-screening operations that the statute’s text and separation-of-powers concerns counsel against. Thuraissigiam reinforces that Congress may tightly limit judicial review for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens, and nothing in the APA can override § 1252’s unmistakable jurisdictional limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-limiting scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 reflects Congress’s intent to confine judicial review of border screening and removal-related processes to the statute’s specified avenues, rather than broad APA suits in district court. Respondents’ requested relief would effectively “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV procedures governing inspection and expedited removal, triggering § 1252(f)(1)’s limit on lower-court injunctive authority as construed in Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Comm. and reinforced by Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez. DHS v. Thuraissigiam underscores that for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens Congress may sharply limit review and that courts should not expand review beyond what the INA authorizes through the APA or generalized constitutional claims. As an institutional matter, adherence to this longstanding statutory structure and precedent counsels dismissal from district court (leaving any review to whatever limited INA mechanisms apply).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of 8 U.S.C. § 1252 reflect Congress’s intent to channel and, in significant measure, preclude district-court review of claims that seek to regulate how DHS conducts border screening and admission decisions, reserving limited review to the INA’s specified mechanisms and, for certain systemic challenges to expedited-removal procedures, to the narrow avenue Congress provided in § 1252(e)(3). Respondents’ APA and constitutional claims, though framed as “front-end” access-to-asylum challenges under 8 U.S.C. § 1158, would in practical effect supervise or constrain DHS’s implementation of removal-screening and processing at or near the border—precisely the kind of litigation § 1252 is designed to prevent from proceeding in district court. DHS v. Thuraissigiam underscores that, for arriving/non-admitted noncitizens, Congress may tightly limit judicial review and that courts should not expand review beyond the procedures Congress authorized, a principle that counsels against reading the APA to supply an alternative route around § 1252’s channeling scheme. Because the INA supplies specific, limited review pathways and § 1252’s jurisdictional limits are best read as controlling, the district court suit should be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s channeling provisions should not be read to categorically bar district-court review of systemic, front-end “turnback” practices that prevent noncitizens from accessing the statutory asylum process in the first place, particularly where there is no removal order, no administrative record, and thus no meaningful path into the petition-for-review scheme. Section 1252(g), as construed in Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, is narrowly limited to claims arising from the specific decisions to “commence proceedings, adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders,” and does not unmistakably strip jurisdiction over challenges to alleged obstruction of access to apply for asylum under 8 U.S.C. § 1158. Likewise, § 1252(b)(9) should not be stretched to swallow all claims merely touching immigration enforcement, especially when doing so would create a practical accountability vacuum inconsistent with procedural fairness; Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it addressed limits on habeas review after expedited-removal screening, not an affirmative bar to initiating the asylum process. With APA review available absent an adequate alternative remedy (5 U.S.C. §§ 702, 704), respondents may proceed at least to litigate whether DHS’s practices unlawfully foreclose the statutory opportunity to seek asylum and violate minimum constitutional constraints.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether noncitizen asylum seekers and an immigrant-rights organization can sue DHS in federal court to challenge alleged policies and practices at or near the U.S.–Mexico border that restrict access to the asylum process, or whether immigration statutes and Supreme Court precedent foreclose such review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the Immigration and Nationality Act’s limits on judicial review and channeling provisions (including jurisdiction-stripping and review-channeling rules applicable to removal/asylum processing), in tension with constitutional due process and habeas principles as invoked through Supreme Court precedent (notably DHS v. Thuraissigiam).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the Secretary of Homeland Security and other federal officials) argue that the challenged conduct is effectively bound up with decisions and processes governing admission, expedited removal, and asylum screening, an area Congress tightly regulated and limited judicial review over; they contend plaintiffs cannot use broad APA/constitutional-style claims to obtain systemic, programmatic relief that would circumvent Congress’s exclusive review scheme and that Supreme Court cases like DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirm that recent entrants at the border have sharply limited constitutional and habeas-based avenues to contest such determinations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Al Otro Lado and associated plaintiffs) argue that they are not seeking impermissible review of individual removal orders but rather to stop unlawful government practices that categorically obstruct access to the statutory asylum process (e.g., turnbacks or other barriers to presenting asylum claims), and that the federal courts retain jurisdiction to hear these claims because jurisdiction-stripping provisions should not be read to insulate systemic illegality; they further contend that Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it involved an individual’s habeas challenge to an expedited removal order seeking additional procedures, not a suit over affirmative interference with the ability to apply for asylum in the first place.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 136 S. Ct. 2090 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the “no forum” concern when alleged turnbacks prevent any § 1225 or § 1158 process from starting, but under a minimalist, text-and-structure approach that policy worry cannot justify creating an implied APA/equitable pathway Congress did not preserve in IIRIRA. Even accepting Justice Sotomayor’s Reno v. AADC point that § 1252(f)(1) is largely remedial, that only sharpens the narrowest available ground for decision: the classwide/systemwide injunction sought here is foreclosed because it would, in practical operation, supervise and regulate the inspection/expedited-removal screening machinery Congress insulated through § 1252(a)(2)(A) and the tightly limited review in § 1252(e). Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) reinforces that Congress provided a specific, cabined mechanism for systemic challenges, which counsels against inferring an additional, free-standing vehicle for closely related programmatic relief. This approach preserves individualized avenues Congress expressly allowed, while avoiding broad district-court management of border-processing policy that threatens institutional legitimacy and runs against Thuraissigiam’s caution about expanding review beyond the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the asserted “no forum” gap when officials allegedly block the statutory process from starting, but under a textualist/originalist approach that policy concern cannot supply jurisdiction Congress withdrew: §1252(a)(2)(A) bars review of claims “arising from” the inspection/expedited-removal machinery “notwithstanding any other provision of law,” and §1252(e) then affirmatively specifies the only review Congress permitted. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on §1252(e)(3) further undercuts the respondents’ position because Congress created a targeted, time- and topic-limited vehicle for systemic challenges, which is powerful evidence that it did not silently preserve a freestanding APA/equitable pathway for closely related “turnback” claims. Justice Sotomayor’s Reno v. AADC point that §1252(f)(1) is principally remedial does not overcome the independent jurisdiction-channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions; at most it reinforces that, even if some adjudication were possible, the particular programmatic injunctive relief sought is foreclosed. Thuraissigiam confirms the baseline that recent entrants at the threshold receive only the process and judicial review Congress provided, and relabeling the dispute as “access” cannot alter the statute’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the hardest point—that alleged “turnbacks” occur before any formal proceeding or order, so § 1252’s channeling could leave “no forum”—but that policy intuition cannot override Congress’s sweeping text barring review of claims “arising from” the inspection/expedited-removal apparatus “notwithstanding any other provision of law.” Even if the challenged conduct is styled as antecedent, the requested relief would in operation supervise and re-engineer how officers conduct § 1225 processing and credible-fear referrals, which is precisely the kind of district-court programmatic control IIRIRA aimed to prevent, as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Reno v. AADC usefully clarifies that § 1252(f)(1) is largely remedial rather than jurisdictional, but that does not overcome the independent jurisdiction-stripping and tightly limited review provisions in § 1252(a)(2)(A) and § 1252(e), nor does it justify implying an APA/equitable pathway where Congress provided a specific systemic mechanism in § 1252(e)(3). Thuraissigiam does not dictate the result, but it reinforces that for recent entrants Congress may sharply confine judicial review—even if that leaves some claims without the broad forum respondents seek.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is structural: IIRIRA was designed to curb district-court, programmatic control over border processing, and §1252(f)(1) powerfully confirms Congress’s intent to restrict broad injunctive remedies. But that does not resolve the antecedent forum question Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson identify: where the alleged practice is categorical turnbacks that prevent any §1158(a)(1)/§1225 process from beginning, §1252(b)(9) and §1252(a)(2)(A) are a poor textual fit because there is no proceeding or determination to channel into, and I do not read “arising from” to clearly create a law-free zone for pre-process obstruction. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on §1252(e)(3) does not persuade me because that provision is narrow and time-limited, aimed at validating the expedited-removal system’s regulations and written directives, not authorizing or insulating ultra vires conduct that blocks access to the statutory scheme altogether. I can accept Roberts’s remedial caution and would tailor relief consistent with §1252(f)(1), but absent a clearer statement I will not read §1252 to foreclose all judicial review for the people least able to trigger Congress’s protections in the first place.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point—that Congress meant to foreclose programmatic district-court supervision of § 1225 processing—is the strongest argument for Petitioners, and it has real force where the relief sought would effectively prescribe border-screening operations. But textually, § 1252(a)(2)(A) and § 1252(b)(9) most naturally reach claims that are reviewable within (or derivative of) the removal/expedited-removal machinery; where the allegation is categorical obstruction that prevents any § 1158(a)(1)/§ 1225 process from commencing, there is nothing to “channel,” and I do not see the clear statement needed to create a jurisdictional vacuum. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) does not move me because that provision’s narrow, time- and topic-limited design for challenges to the validity of the expedited-removal “system” is poor evidence that Congress also silently displaced threshold ultra vires access claims; instead it suggests Congress knew how to speak precisely when it wished to make a pathway exclusive. I agree with Justice Sotomayor (invoking Reno v. AADC) that § 1252(f)(1) can sharply constrain classwide injunctions, but that remedial limitation supports narrowing the remedy rather than denying jurisdiction to hear a threshold access claim at all.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: that alleged “turnbacks” occur before any proceeding or order, creating a “no forum” problem. But under a textualist approach, that equitable concern cannot overcome Congress’s unmistakably broad preclusion in § 1252(a)(2)(A) (“notwithstanding any other provision of law”) for claims “arising from” the § 1225 inspection/expedited-removal machinery, paired with the affirmative, narrowly specified review Congress authorized in § 1252(e). Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point reinforces this: respondents’ programmatic injunction would, in operation, supervise the very screening and referral process Congress chose to insulate from district-court control, and § 1252(e)(3)’s specific, time-limited mechanism for systemic challenges is hard to reconcile with an implied, freestanding APA/equitable pathway. Reno v. AADC, as Justice Sotomayor invokes, may characterize § 1252(f)(1) as remedial, but it does not supply jurisdiction where §§ 1252(a)(2)(A) and 1252(e) withhold it, nor does it justify judicially creating a forum Congress declined to provide.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson raise the strongest point—the feared “no forum” gap when alleged turnbacks occur before any § 1225/expedited-removal proceeding starts—but under the text and structure Congress enacted in IIRIRA, that policy concern cannot justify implying a free-standing district-court APA/equitable cause of action that would, in practical effect, supervise the inspection and credible-fear machinery. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1252(a)(2)(A)’s “notwithstanding any other provision of law” bar, § 1252(g) as construed in Reno v. AADC, and Congress’s inclusion of the narrow systemic-review mechanism in § 1252(e)(3) together strongly indicate Congress chose limited, specific avenues for review and foreclosed broader programmatic litigation. Thuraissigiam reinforces the historical/institutional baseline that for recent entrants Congress may specify—and limit—the process and judicial review available even if that leaves some claims without the broader forum respondents prefer. I agree with Justice Sotomayor that § 1252(f)(1) is largely remedial, but even setting that aside, the independent channeling and preclusion provisions still block the systemwide injunction sought here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson’s “no forum/antecedent obstruction” argument is the hardest because it highlights conduct that allegedly occurs before any formal proceeding or order exists to channel into review. But on the text Congress enacted, § 1252(a)(2)(A)’s “notwithstanding any other provision of law” and its reach to claims “arising from” the inspection/expedited-removal machinery, together with § 1252(e)’s sharply delimited review and § 1252(e)(3)’s specific avenue for systemic challenges, indicate Congress chose to foreclose freestanding district-court APA/equitable supervision even if that leaves some claims without the forum respondents prefer—structural specificity is strong evidence against implying an additional pathway, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes. Justice Sotomayor’s Reno v. AADC point that § 1252(f)(1) is largely remedial rather than jurisdictional is important, but it does not defeat the independent jurisdiction-channeling and review-limiting provisions doing the primary work here; at most it suggests we should be careful to ground disposition in the jurisdictional bars rather than overreading (f)(1). Thuraissigiam reinforces the baseline original-meaning understanding that recent entrants at the threshold receive only the process and review Congress provided, and relabeling the challenge as “access” cannot expand jurisdiction where the statute’s text and structure withdraw it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point—that IIRIRA is a “tightly reticulated” scheme designed to prevent district-court programmatic supervision of § 1225 processing—matters a great deal, and I accept (with Justice Sotomayor’s Reno v. AADC framing) that § 1252(f)(1) can sharply limit the form and breadth of injunctive relief. But Roberts’s structural argument still assumes the challenged conduct is part of, or at least tethered to, an inspection/expedited-removal “determination” that can trigger § 1252(a)(2)(A) or be channeled by § 1252(b)(9); the respondents’ core allegation is antecedent obstruction that prevents the statutory screening and asylum-application mechanisms from starting at all. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) does not persuade me to treat that narrow, time- and subject-limited review provision as an implicit clear statement creating a no-forum zone for ultra vires turnbacks that short-circuit § 1158(a)(1) before any § 1225(b)(1) implementation decision is made. Under a pragmatic, procedure-focused lens, I cannot read these provisions to foreclose all judicial testing of categorical illegality at the threshold absent clearer congressional language, even if the eventual remedy must be carefully cabined.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress in IIRIRA erected a tightly reticulated scheme channeling and limiting judicial review over admission, expedited removal, and asylum screening, and plaintiffs may not repackage challenges bound up with those processes as systemic APA-style claims to obtain programmatic injunctive relief outside that scheme. DHS v. Thuraissigiam underscores both IIRIRA’s central aim to protect Executive discretion from “undue interference by the courts” and the sharply limited constitutional and habeas-based avenues available to recent entrants at the border seeking to expand procedures. To the extent respondents seek broad injunctions that would effectively restrain the operation of Part IV provisions such as 8 U.S.C. § 1225, § 1252(f)(1) further limits lower courts’ authority to issue such relief, and Reno v. AADC confirms these IIRIRA limits are to be applied as Congress wrote them. A narrow disposition is appropriate: whatever room may exist for individual relief, this suit for systemwide injunctive intervention is foreclosed by the INA’s review-channeling and remedy-limiting provisions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and restricts judicial review over expedited-removal and related asylum-screening matters, and § 1252(a)(2)(A) together with § 1252(e)(2)–(5) reflects Congress’s deliberate choice to foreclose broad, programmatic federal-court review outside the exclusive scheme it created. Under a textualist reading, respondents’ APA-style systemic challenge would functionally “circumvent Congress’s exclusive review scheme” by inviting lower courts to supervise border screening and admission practices that are inseparable from determinations Congress committed to limited review. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that recent entrants apprehended at or near the border have sharply constrained habeas/due-process avenues to obtain additional process beyond what Congress authorized, and it counsels against expanding jurisdiction where Congress has expressly narrowed it. Because the statutes plainly strip jurisdiction in this area, any relief must come through the review channels Congress specified, not a freestanding district-court suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions—especially 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(5) and § 1252(b)(9), together with the limited review permitted for expedited removal in § 1252(e)(2)—reflect Congress’s choice to confine judicial review of claims bound up with admission, expedited removal, and asylum screening to the statute’s exclusive scheme. Respondents’ APA- and constitutional-framed request for systemic, programmatic relief would operate as an indirect means of reviewing and supervising those removal/asylum-screening determinations, which § 1252 broadly precludes “by any other provision of law.” DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that recent entrants apprehended near the border have sharply limited constitutional and habeas avenues to demand additional process beyond what Congress provided, and it cautions against expanding review in this domain. Practical consequences also counsel restraint: permitting district-court classwide injunctions over border processing would undermine uniform administration and the enforcement interests Congress sought to protect through § 1252’s comprehensive review scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s jurisdiction-stripping and channeling provisions should not be read to insulate systemic, categorical interference with the ability to apply for asylum at all, as opposed to review of individual removal orders or discretionary prosecutorial choices. Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Comm. makes clear that 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) is “nothing more or less than a limit on injunctive relief,” not a wholesale bar to federal-court jurisdiction over unlawful policies; absent an “unmistakable legislative command,” courts retain equitable authority to remedy ongoing statutory violations. Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it addressed an individual habeas challenge seeking additional procedures after an expedited removal determination, whereas this suit targets affirmative practices (e.g., turnbacks) that prevent access to the statutory asylum process in the first instance. Given the practical consequences for vulnerable asylum seekers and the need to ensure access to congressionally created protections, federal courts may hear these claims even if the ultimate remedy must respect § 1252(f)(1)’s limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions in §1252(a)(2) and §1252(b)(9) are textually aimed at review of "removal" decisions and the process of adjudicating particular cases, not at claims that officials are categorically preventing noncitizens from ever accessing the statutory screening and asylum application process Congress created in §1158(a)(1) and §1225(b). Reading §1252 to bar all systemic challenges to alleged turnbacks or obstruction would create serious workability problems by insulating ultra vires practices from any judicial forum and would stretch §1252(b)(9)’s "arising from" language beyond its coherent role as a channeling rule for claims that can be meaningfully raised within removal proceedings. Thuraissigiam involved an individual habeas challenge seeking additional procedures after an expedited removal order and does not resolve whether federal courts may hear an APA/constitutional-style challenge to affirmative interference with the ability to apply for asylum in the first place. Consistent with the domestic-application analysis reflected in RJR Nabisco (and distinguishing Sale), the alleged conduct at or effectively at the port of entry can be treated as occurring within the statute’s focus and is not barred on extraterritoriality grounds.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and sharply limits judicial review of border-admission and expedited-removal/asylum-screening matters, and respondents’ effort to repackage those disputes as “policies and practices” claims would circumvent Congress’s exclusive scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252, including the narrow avenue in § 1252(e)(3) for certain systemic challenges. Where Congress has spoken in jurisdiction-stripping and channeling terms, we must respect that allocation of authority rather than enlarge equitable or APA review to reach programmatic relief that effectively second-guesses frontline inadmissibility and screening decisions. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that recent entrants at the border have only the limited review Congress provided and that broader constitutional/habeas-style demands for additional process are foreclosed. Whatever the merits of the alleged turnbacks, the proper forum and mechanism must be the one Congress prescribed in § 1252, not a freestanding federal-court action seeking sweeping injunctive relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Congress in the INA tightly channeled and limited judicial review of decisions and processes bound up with inspection, expedited removal, and the initiation/execution of removal proceedings, including through § 1252(g) and related review-channeling provisions. Under Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, § 1252(g) must be read to bar suits that "arise from" the decision to commence proceedings, adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders, and respondents’ requested systemic injunction would functionally supervise and constrain those protected enforcement/processing choices rather than merely remedy a discrete, collateral illegality. DHS v. Thuraissigiam reinforces that recent entrants at the border have sharply limited constitutional/habeas avenues to demand additional process beyond what Congress provided, counseling judicial restraint and adherence to the statutory scheme. Practical workability and institutional concerns also cut against creating an APA-style path for programmatic border-asylum litigation that would circumvent Congress’s exclusive review framework and invite widespread, difficult-to-administer injunctions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme, including 8 U.S.C. § 1252(e)(2) and § 1252(e)(5), reflects Congress’s choice to sharply limit and channel review of expedited-removal and closely related screening determinations, allowing only narrow habeas inquiries into status, order, and identity. Respondents’ requested systemic relief—aimed at changing DHS’s border practices governing access to inspection and asylum screening—would effectively circumvent that exclusive scheme by inviting programmatic APA/constitutional review in district court notwithstanding Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that recent entrants subject to expedited-removal procedures have severely constrained habeas and due-process avenues beyond what Congress provided, and its reasoning counsels against expanding judicial review through reframing the claim as “systemic” rather than order-specific. While respondents characterize their suit as independent of individual removal orders, the text and structure of § 1252’s channeling provisions indicate that challenges bound up with the admission/expedited-removal/asylum-screening process must proceed, if at all, only through the limited statutory routes Congress authorized.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions—particularly 8 U.S.C. § 1252(e)(2)–(5) and § 1252(a)(2)—are best read to bar review of individual expedited-removal determinations and the procedures used to reach them, not to insulate alleged categorical, affirmative interference with the statutory ability to apply for asylum at all. DHS v. Thuraissigiam involved an individual habeas attack on the adequacy of expedited-removal screening and sought additional process after an adverse determination, whereas this suit challenges alleged turnbacks and access barriers that precede and obstruct the initiation of the asylum process, making it meaningfully distinct from indirect review of a removal order. Reading § 1252 to foreclose any systemic “access-to-asylum” challenge would create a serious procedural-fairness gap by permitting unlawful executive practices to evade judicial scrutiny entirely, a result courts should avoid absent clear congressional command. While the Government may later invoke limits like § 1252(f)(1) on the form of injunctive relief, those constraints do not categorically eliminate federal-court jurisdiction to hear claims of ongoing systemic illegality.
